concepts.name: Minimum stack
concepts.statement: Store each stack entry as a pair (value, minimum of this entry and everything below it); the stack minimum is then the top pair's second field, and push/pop stay O(1).

concepts.name: Minimum queue via a monotonic deque
concepts.statement: Keep only the elements that can still become the minimum, in non-decreasing order: before pushing x, remove trailing elements larger than x; the head is the minimum and every element is pushed and popped at most once, so operations are amortised O(1). Removal needs the value (method 1) or stored indices (method 2).

concepts.name: Queue from two stacks (with minimum)
concepts.statement: Push to stack s1 and pop from stack s2, moving all of s1 into s2 when s2 is empty; each element moves once, so all operations are amortised O(1), and with minimum stacks the queue minimum is the smaller of the two stack minima.

concepts.name: Sliding window minimum
concepts.statement: The minimum of every length-M subarray of an array of length N can be found in O(N) total by sliding a minimum queue along the array.
aliases: minimum of all subarrays of fixed length

concepts.name: Sparse table
concepts.statement: A table st[i][j] holding the answer for the range [j, j+2^i-1], built in O(N log N) from st[i][j] = f(st[i-1][j], st[i-1][j+2^(i-1)]); it serves range queries on an immutable array.

concepts.name: Sparse table range query by power-of-two decomposition
concepts.statement: Any range splits into at most ceil(log2 length) disjoint power-of-two blocks, so an associative query (e.g. sum) is answered in O(log N) by combining those blocks from largest to smallest.

concepts.name: O(1) range minimum with a sparse table
concepts.statement: For an idempotent operation such as min, a range [L,R] is covered by two overlapping blocks of length 2^k with k = floor(log2(R-L+1)), giving O(1) queries after O(N log N) preprocessing.
concepts.notes: also covers precomputed vs on-the-fly log2

concepts.name: Structures for O(1) associative range queries
concepts.statement: The overlapping-block trick needs idempotence; disjoint sparse tables and sqrt trees answer any associative range query in O(1).
concepts.notes: pointer only; disjoint sparse table is linked externally

concepts.name: Disjoint set union
concepts.statement: A structure over disjoint sets with make_set, union_sets and find_set (returns a representative), stored as a forest of parent pointers whose roots are the representatives.

concepts.name: Path compression
concepts.statement: During find_set, re-point every visited vertex directly to the root; alone this gives O(log n) average per call.

concepts.name: Union by size / rank
concepts.statement: Attach the root of the smaller (by size or by depth bound) tree under the larger; without path compression this already bounds operations at O(log n).
concepts.notes: also: linking by index works, coin-flip linking does not (#linking-by-index-coin-flip-linking)

concepts.name: DSU amortised complexity is O(alpha(n))
concepts.statement: With path compression and union by size/rank, a sequence of operations costs O(alpha(n)) amortised each, alpha the inverse Ackermann function (at most 4 for practical n); stated without proof, with Fredman-Saks lower bound in the history.
concepts.notes: amortised complexity is defined in passing

concepts.name: DSU for incremental connectivity
concepts.statement: Adding edges as unions and answering 'same component?' with find_set handles an incrementally built graph in near-constant time per operation; also used for components of an image and in Kruskal.

concepts.name: Painting subarrays offline with DSU
concepts.statement: Process repaint queries in reverse, with each cell's DSU parent pointing to the next unpainted cell, so every cell is painted exactly once and skipped thereafter.

concepts.name: DSU with distance/parity to the representative
concepts.statement: Store each node's distance (or parity) to its parent and fix it up during path compression; with parity this checks online whether components stay bipartite as edges are added.

concepts.name: Arpa's trick: offline RMQ with DSU
concepts.statement: Sweeping right, link each element to the next smaller element to its right via DSU; the answer to query (L,R) with R = current index is a[find_set(L)], giving O(alpha(n)) per query offline.

concepts.name: Small-to-large merging
concepts.statement: Always merge the smaller collection into the larger: each element moves O(log n) times, so explicit-list DSU costs O(m + n log n), and the same idea merges per-subtree sets in O(n log^2 n).

concepts.name: Fenwick tree
concepts.statement: An array T where T[i] stores f over A[g(i)..i], g(i) clearing the trailing 1 bits of i (0-based; i & (i+1)); prefix queries follow i -> g(i)-1 and updates follow i -> i | (i+1), each O(log N), for a group operation f.

concepts.name: Fenwick tree for point update, range sum
concepts.statement: Implement sum(r) and add(i, delta) and answer [l,r] as sum(r) - sum(l-1); one-based variant uses i & -i (toggle the last set bit).

concepts.name: Linear-time Fenwick construction
concepts.statement: Build in O(N) by adding a[i] into T[i] and pushing T[i] once to its parent range i | (i+1).

concepts.name: Fenwick tree for prefix minimum
concepts.statement: With min (not a group) a Fenwick tree can answer only prefix-minimum queries and only under decreasing updates.

concepts.name: Fenwick range update with point / range query
concepts.statement: Range add [l,r] by x becomes add(l,x), add(r+1,-x) on a difference array, so a prefix sum gives a point value; two BITs B1, B2 with sum(B1,i)*i - sum(B2,i) give range-update range-query.

concepts.name: Sqrt decomposition for range queries
concepts.statement: Split the array into ~sqrt(n) blocks with precomputed block aggregates; a query sums two partial tails and whole blocks in O(sqrt n), and the scheme extends to range updates with per-block lazy values.
concepts.notes: article ends with 12 practice-problem links; variants at #other-problems

concepts.name: Mo's algorithm
concepts.statement: Answer offline range queries by sorting them by (block of left end, right end) and moving a window with add/remove; total O((N+Q) F sqrt N) for add/remove cost F.

concepts.name: Segment tree
concepts.statement: A binary tree over array segments, each node storing the merge of its two halves (e.g. a sum), stored implicitly in an array with children 2v and 2v+1 in at most 4n cells.

concepts.name: Segment tree range query and point update
concepts.statement: A range query visits O(log n) nodes (fully-inside nodes return stored values, disjoint ones contribute nothing); a point update changes one node per level, also O(log n).

concepts.name: Segment tree with custom node values
concepts.statement: Change what a node stores and how children merge: maximum, maximum with count, gcd/lcm, or the four values (sum, best prefix, best suffix, best) for maximum subsegment sum.

concepts.name: Searching by descending the segment tree
concepts.statement: Find the k-th zero, the first prefix reaching a sum, or the first element above x in a range in O(log n) by walking down using child aggregates, instead of O(log^2 n) binary search over queries.

concepts.name: Merge sort tree
concepts.statement: Store each node's segment sorted (built by merging children); a lower-bound query over a range takes O(log^2 n), with multisets for updates and O(log n) with fractional cascading.

concepts.name: Lazy propagation
concepts.statement: For range updates, store a pending update at fully covered nodes and push it to the children only when a later operation descends there, keeping range add/assign with range queries at O(log n).

concepts.name: 2D segment tree
concepts.statement: A segment tree over rows whose nodes are segment trees over columns answers submatrix queries in O(log n log m); for sparse points the inner trees are built only over the points in each node.

concepts.name: Persistent segment tree
concepts.statement: An update copies only the O(log n) nodes on its path, keeping every past version; with versions over prefixes of values, the k-th smallest in a range is found in O(log n).

concepts.name: Dynamic (implicit) segment tree
concepts.statement: Create nodes lazily on first access so a tree over a huge index range uses memory proportional to the operations performed.

concepts.name: Treap
concepts.statement: A binary tree on pairs (key X, priority Y) that is a BST in X and a heap in Y; with random priorities its expected height is O(log N), and distinct priorities fix the shape uniquely.

concepts.name: Treap split and merge
concepts.statement: split(T, X) cuts a treap into keys <= X and > X, merge(T1, T2) joins treaps whose keys are ordered; both are O(log N) expected and insert, erase, build and union are written with them.

concepts.name: Building a treap in O(N) offline
concepts.statement: From sorted keys (or sorted (x,y) pairs, using a stack) a treap / Cartesian tree is built in linear time.

concepts.name: Implicit treap
concepts.statement: Use subtree sizes as implicit keys so a treap acts as an array supporting insert/erase anywhere, range aggregates, range add/paint and range reversal in O(log N).

concepts.name: Sqrt tree
concepts.statement: Recursively apply sqrt decomposition (prefixOp, suffixOp, between) to get a tree of height O(log log n); with power-of-two block sizes, any associative range query is O(1) after O(n log log n) preprocessing.

concepts.name: Sqrt tree updates
concepts.statement: Point updates in O(sqrt n) by indexing the root's between array with a nested sqrt tree; segment assignment with lazy marks in O(sqrt n log log n) or O(sqrt n) depending on which layers may be lazy.

concepts.name: Randomized meldable heap
concepts.statement: A heap-ordered binary tree where every operation reduces to merge, which keeps the smaller root and recursively merges into a randomly chosen child; operations run in expected O(log n) with high probability.

concepts.name: Random root-to-leaf path length bound
concepts.statement: The expected length of a random root-to-leaf walk in any binary tree with n vertices is at most log(n+1) (induction), and it exceeds (c+1) log n with probability at most n^-c, so random-child merge is O(log n) with high probability.

concepts.name: Offline deletion via segment tree over time
concepts.statement: Give each element its lifetime interval over the query sequence, insert it into the O(log n) segment-tree nodes covering that interval, and DFS the tree with rollback, so a structure with add in O(T(n)) supports deletion in O(T(n) log n) offline.

concepts.name: Undoing operations with a change stack (rollback DSU)
concepts.statement: A structure whose updates are worst-case O(T(n)) can be rolled back in O(T(n)) by pushing each modified cell's old value on a stack; DSU with union by rank but no path compression supports this, giving offline dynamic connectivity. Rollbacks break amortised bounds.

concepts.name: Dynamic programming: reuse of overlapping subproblems
concepts.statement: A recursion whose calls repeat the same subproblems (naive Fibonacci makes O(2^n) calls) can be made polynomial by computing each of its distinct subproblems once.
concepts.notes: article ends with 8 practice-problem links plus DP contest links

concepts.name: Memoization (top-down DP)
concepts.statement: Cache each subproblem's answer in a lookup table (an array when states are small integers, a map otherwise) and return it on repeat calls, turning Fibonacci into O(n) calls.

concepts.name: Bottom-up (tabulated) DP
concepts.statement: Fill the table from the base cases upward in dependency order; when a state needs only the last few states, keep only those for O(1) memory.

concepts.name: Classic DP problems
concepts.statement: Standard first DP problems: 0-1 knapsack, subset sum, longest increasing subsequence, counting grid paths, longest common subsequence, edit distance.
concepts.notes: table only; subset sum, grid paths, LCS, edit distance have no article here

concepts.name: 0-1 knapsack
concepts.statement: With f[i][j] the best value from the first i items within capacity j, f[i][j] = max(f[i-1][j], f[i-1][j-w_i] + v_i), solvable in O(nW).

concepts.name: One-dimensional knapsack and iteration order
concepts.statement: Drop the item dimension: iterate capacity downward for 0-1 knapsack (each item once) and upward for complete knapsack (unbounded reuse); the same update with the wrong order solves the other problem.

concepts.name: Complete (unbounded) knapsack
concepts.statement: With unlimited copies, f[i][j] = max(f[i-1][j], f[i][j-w_i] + v_i), O(nW).

concepts.name: Bounded knapsack by binary grouping
concepts.statement: Split k_i copies into bundles of 1, 2, 4, ... plus a remainder so every count up to k_i is a sum of bundles; the bounded problem becomes 0-1 knapsack in O(W sum log k_i).

concepts.name: Bounded knapsack by monotone queue
concepts.statement: Group capacities by residue mod w_i; each transition becomes a sliding-window maximum, giving O(nW).

concepts.name: LIS in O(n^2)
concepts.statement: d[i] = 1 + max d[j] over j < i with a[j] < a[i] is the length of the longest increasing subsequence ending at i; the answer is max d[i].

concepts.name: Restoring a DP solution with parent pointers
concepts.statement: Record for each state which predecessor achieved its optimum, then follow the pointers back from the best final state; alternatively recompute the choice to save memory.

concepts.name: LIS in O(n log n) with binary search
concepts.statement: Keep d[l] = smallest tail of an increasing subsequence of length l; d is sorted and each element updates one entry found by binary search (lower bound), giving O(n log n).

concepts.name: LIS with a prefix-maximum structure
concepts.statement: Process values in order and compute d[i] as one plus a prefix maximum over smaller values held in a segment or Fenwick tree (after coordinate compression); extends to counting LIS.

concepts.name: LIS variants: non-decreasing, counting, covering
concepts.statement: Non-decreasing needs only upper bound; the number of LIS sums ways over optimal predecessors; the minimum number of non-increasing subsequences covering a sequence equals the LIS length (duality proof).

concepts.name: Monotone optimal split point
concepts.statement: opt(i, j), the smallest k minimising the transition for dp(i, j), is monotone: opt(i, j) <= opt(i, j+1); this is the precondition that divide-and-conquer DP relies on.

concepts.name: Divide and conquer DP optimization
concepts.statement: For dp(i,j) = min_k dp(i-1,k-1) + C(k,j) with monotone optimal split opt(i,j) in j, compute a row by solving the middle j and recursing with narrowed k ranges, in O(n log n) per row instead of O(n^2).

concepts.name: Quadrangle inequality
concepts.statement: C(a,c) + C(b,d) <= C(a,d) + C(b,c) for a <= b <= c <= d; with monotonicity it implies monotone optimal splits, the precondition for D&C and Knuth optimizations.

concepts.name: Knuth's optimization
concepts.statement: For range DP dp(i,j) = min over i<=k<j of dp(i,k) + dp(k+1,j) + C(i,j), if C satisfies the quadrangle inequality and monotonicity then opt(i,j-1) <= opt(i,j) <= opt(i+1,j), so restricting k reduces O(n^3) to O(n^2).
concepts.notes: article ends with 4 practice-problem links; proof at #proof-of-correctness

concepts.name: DP on broken profile
concepts.statement: Tile a grid row by row with state (row, bitmask of cells already filled in the next row) to count or optimise domino-type fillings, e.g. the 'Parquet' problem.
concepts.notes: article ends with 13 practice-problem links; prose is very short

concepts.name: Largest zero submatrix in O(nm)
concepts.statement: For each cell compute d[i][j], the nearest row above with a 1; then in each row the widest rectangle bounded by d is found with a monotonic stack (nearest larger d to left and right), giving O(nm) time and O(m) memory.

concepts.name: Nearest smaller element to the left/right with a stack
concepts.statement: Scan the row keeping a stack of indices with increasing values, popping while the top is not smaller; the remaining top is the nearest smaller (here: larger d) index, O(m) per row amortised.

concepts.name: Polynomial rolling hash of a string
concepts.statement: hash(s) = sum s[i] p^i mod m, with p a prime near the alphabet size (e.g. 31) and m a large prime (e.g. 1e9+9); equal strings have equal hashes and unequal ones collide with probability about 1/m.

concepts.name: Grouping duplicate strings by hash
concepts.statement: Hash every string, sort hashes with indices, and group equal hashes, finding duplicates in O(nm + n log n) instead of O(nm log n).

concepts.name: Substring hash from prefix hashes
concepts.statement: With prefix hashes, hash(s[i..j]) * p^i = H[j+1] - H[i]; compare two substrings by multiplying both to a common power (or using a modular inverse) in O(1).

concepts.name: Counting distinct substrings by hashing
concepts.statement: For each length l, collect the normalised hashes of all length-l substrings and count distinct values; O(n^2 log n).

concepts.name: Collision probability and double hashing
concepts.statement: Comparing one string against many raises collision odds roughly to (number of comparisons)/m by the birthday effect; using two independent moduli (or one 64-bit modulus) makes collisions negligible.

concepts.name: Rabin-Karp string matching
concepts.statement: Compare the pattern's hash with the hash of every length-|s| window of the text computed from prefix hashes, finding all occurrences in O(|s| + |t|).
concepts.notes: article ends with 4 practice-problem links; very short article

concepts.name: Prefix function
concepts.statement: pi[i] is the length of the longest proper prefix of s[0..i] that is also a suffix of it; pi[0] = 0.

concepts.name: Computing the prefix function in O(n)
concepts.statement: Since pi[i+1] <= pi[i] + 1, and on a mismatch the next candidate length is pi[j-1], following these links computes the whole array in O(n) amortised, online.

concepts.name: Knuth-Morris-Pratt substring search
concepts.statement: Compute the prefix function of s + # + t; every position in the t part with pi = |s| ends an occurrence, so all occurrences are found in O(|s| + |t|) time and O(|s|) memory.

concepts.name: Counting occurrences of each prefix
concepts.statement: Count how often each prefix occurs by tallying pi values and propagating counts along pi links from long to short.

concepts.name: Shortest period / string compression
concepts.statement: With k = n - pi[n-1], if k divides n then s is a repetition of its prefix of length k (the shortest such); otherwise no compression exists. The Z-function gives the same answer.

concepts.name: KMP automaton
concepts.statement: Precompute transitions (state = current pi value, next character) for s + # so the text is processed with O(1) per character without storing it; built in O(n k).

concepts.name: Counting distinct substrings incrementally
concepts.statement: When appending c to s, the new substrings are the suffixes of s+c longer than the maximum prefix function (or Z) value of reverse(s+c); summing gives O(n^2) overall.

concepts.name: Z-function
concepts.statement: z[i] is the length of the longest common prefix of s and the suffix s[i..]; z[0] is taken as 0.

concepts.name: Computing the Z-function in O(n)
concepts.statement: Maintain the rightmost match segment [l, r); for i < r start from min(r - i, z[i - l]) and extend naively; every extension step moves r right, so the total is O(n).

concepts.name: Pattern search with the Z-function
concepts.statement: Compute Z of p + separator + t; positions in the t part with z = |p| are occurrences, in O(|p| + |t|).

concepts.name: Suffix array
concepts.statement: The array of starting indices of all suffixes of s in lexicographic order.

concepts.name: Suffix array by prefix doubling in O(n log n)
concepts.statement: Sort cyclic shifts of s + $ by their first 2^k characters, using equivalence classes from round k and counting sort on pairs, for log n rounds; this yields the suffix array.

concepts.name: Substring search and comparison with a suffix array
concepts.statement: Binary search the suffix array for a pattern in O(|p| log |t|); keeping the doubling rounds' class arrays compares any two substrings in O(1) and gives LCP in O(log n).

concepts.name: LCP array (Kasai)
concepts.statement: The LCP of adjacent sorted suffixes is computed in O(n) because the LCP drops by at most one moving from suffix i to suffix i+1; the LCP of any two suffixes is then a range minimum.

concepts.name: Distinct substrings from suffix array and LCP
concepts.statement: The number of distinct substrings is sum over sorted suffixes of (n - p[i]) - lcp[i-1].

concepts.name: Trie
concepts.statement: A rooted tree whose edges carry letters with distinct labels out of each vertex; each vertex is the string spelled from the root, marked if it ends a dictionary word; insertion is O(length).

concepts.name: Aho-Corasick automaton
concepts.statement: Turn a trie into a DFA with suffix links (to the longest proper suffix that is a trie vertex) and transitions computed lazily or by BFS in O(mk); for one pattern this is KMP.

concepts.name: Multi-pattern search with Aho-Corasick
concepts.statement: Feed the text through the automaton and report matches via output (dictionary-suffix) links, in O(len + number of matches).

concepts.name: Search and DP over the Aho-Corasick automaton
concepts.statement: Problems on strings avoiding or containing dictionary words become paths in the automaton: avoid output states for the smallest non-matching string, BFS over (state, mask) for the shortest superstring, DFS over (state, length, count).

concepts.name: Suffix tree (Ukkonen's algorithm)
concepts.statement: Ukkonen's algorithm builds a suffix tree of s in O(n log k) for alphabet size k; code only.
concepts.notes: stub article (says so itself): code only, no explanation; 1 practice-problem link

concepts.name: Suffix automaton
concepts.statement: The minimal DFA accepting all suffixes of s; every path from the initial state spells a substring of s and every substring is one such path.

concepts.name: endpos classes and suffix links
concepts.statement: States correspond to classes of substrings with equal end-position sets; each class holds suffixes of its longest member of consecutive lengths, and the suffix link points to the class of the next shorter suffix, forming a tree.

concepts.name: Online linear-time suffix automaton construction
concepts.statement: Add characters one at a time, creating a state, walking suffix links to add transitions, and cloning a state when a transition is non-continuous; total time O(n log k) with map transitions, O(n) for constant alphabet.

concepts.name: Suffix automaton size bounds
concepts.statement: A suffix automaton of a length-n string has at most 2n-1 states (n >= 2) and at most 3n-4 transitions (n >= 3).

concepts.name: Suffix automaton applications
concepts.statement: Occurrence checks, counting distinct substrings and their total length (DP over the DAG), k-th substring, occurrence counts and positions, shortest absent string and longest common substring of two or many strings.

concepts.name: Lyndon word and Lyndon factorization
concepts.statement: A string is simple (Lyndon) if it is strictly smaller than all its proper suffixes (equivalently, all its nontrivial cyclic shifts); every string factors uniquely as w1 w2 ... wk of simple strings with w1 >= w2 >= ... >= wk.

concepts.name: Duval's algorithm
concepts.statement: A greedy scan over s = s1 s2 s3 (s2 pre-simple) emits the Lyndon factorization in O(n) time and O(1) extra memory.

concepts.name: Smallest cyclic shift
concepts.statement: The lexicographically least rotation starts at the last Lyndon factor of s + s that begins in the first half, found in O(n) by Duval; the suffix array and suffix automaton give alternatives.

concepts.name: Reverse Polish notation evaluation
concepts.statement: Evaluate postfix expressions with one stack: push operands, and for an operator pop its arguments and push the result, in O(n).

concepts.name: Infix expression parsing with two stacks
concepts.statement: Keep an operand stack and an operator stack in strictly decreasing priority; on each operator first apply stacked operators of higher (or equal, for left-associative) priority, handling parentheses as barriers; evaluates in O(n).

concepts.name: Unary and right-associative operators in parsing
concepts.statement: An operator is unary if it follows another operator, an opening parenthesis or nothing; right-associative operators are postponed when priorities are equal.

concepts.name: Palindrome radii d_odd and d_even
concepts.statement: All palindromic substrings are described compactly by, for each center, the number of palindromes centered there (d_odd[i], d_even[i]), since palindromes with a common center are nested.

concepts.name: Manacher's algorithm
concepts.statement: Keep the rightmost found palindrome (l, r); for i inside it start from the mirror's value min(r - i, d[l + r - i]) and extend naively; every extension moves r right, so all radii take O(n).
concepts.notes: trivial O(n^2) center expansion at #trivial-algorithm; linear proof at #complexity-of-manachers-algorithm

concepts.name: Manacher with interleaved separators
concepts.statement: Insert # between characters so even palindromes become odd ones; d[2i] and d[2i+1] recover d_even and d_odd from one odd-only pass.

concepts.name: Repetitions (squares) in a string
concepts.statement: A repetition is a substring of the form tt; a string can contain O(n^2) of them, but they group into O(n) runs described by 4-tuples.

concepts.name: Main-Lorentz algorithm
concepts.statement: Divide and conquer: recurse on halves, then find repetitions crossing the middle as tuples using Z-functions of the halves and reversed halves (left and right crossing criteria), in O(n log n) overall.

concepts.name: Breadth-first search
concepts.statement: From a source, process vertices from a FIFO queue, marking and enqueuing unvisited neighbours; vertices are visited in order of distance, so BFS gives shortest paths by edge count in an unweighted graph in O(n + m).
concepts.notes: article ends with 25 practice-problem links; code in C++ and Java

concepts.name: Restoring BFS shortest paths
concepts.statement: Record each vertex's parent when it is first reached and follow parents back from the target, then reverse.

concepts.name: Applications of BFS
concepts.statement: BFS also finds connected components, least-move solutions of puzzles/games as state graphs, the shortest cycle in a directed graph, the vertices/edges on some shortest a-b path, shortest even-length walks (on a doubled state graph), and shortest paths with 0/1 weights.

concepts.name: Depth-first search
concepts.statement: Recursively visit each unvisited neighbour before backtracking; reaches all vertices reachable from the start in O(n + m) and finds the lexicographically first paths.

concepts.name: DFS entry/exit times and ancestor test
concepts.statement: Record entry and exit times (and white/grey/black colours) during DFS; in a tree, i is an ancestor of j iff tin[i] < tin[j] and tout[i] > tout[j], checkable in O(1).

concepts.name: Classification of edges by DFS
concepts.statement: Edges are tree, back, forward or cross edges according to the endpoints' colours and entry/exit times; undirected graphs have only tree and back edges.

concepts.name: Connected components by repeated DFS/BFS
concepts.statement: Run DFS (or BFS) from each still-unvisited vertex; each run labels one component, all in O(n + m).
concepts.notes: article ends with 3 practice-problem links; thin, mostly overlaps BFS/DFS applications

concepts.name: Iterative DFS with an explicit stack
concepts.statement: Replace recursion with a heap-allocated stack to avoid stack overflow on deep graphs.

concepts.name: Bridge (cut edge)
concepts.statement: An edge of an undirected graph whose removal increases the number of connected components.

concepts.name: Low-link values
concepts.statement: low[v] = min of tin[v], tin[p] over back edges (v,p), and low[to] over DFS-tree children; it is the earliest entry time reachable from v's subtree by one back edge.

concepts.name: Finding bridges in O(N + M)
concepts.statement: A DFS tree edge (v, to) is a bridge iff low[to] > tin[v]; skip only the edge to the parent (by edge index, to allow multi-edges).

concepts.name: Online bridge finding with 2-edge-connected components
concepts.statement: Maintain the forest of 2-edge-connected components with two DSUs (components and 2ECCs) plus explicit parent pointers; a new edge either joins trees (re-rooting the smaller) or compresses the tree path between its ends into one 2ECC, in O(n log n + m) (the article's simplified DSU gives O(n log n + m log n)).

concepts.name: Articulation point (cut vertex)
concepts.statement: A vertex whose removal, with its incident edges, increases the number of connected components of an undirected graph.

concepts.name: Articulation points in O(N + M)
concepts.statement: A non-root v is a cut vertex iff some DFS child to has low[to] >= tin[v]; the root is one iff it has more than one DFS child.

concepts.name: Strongly connected component and condensation
concepts.statement: A maximal vertex set of a directed graph with paths both ways between every pair; contracting each SCC gives the condensation graph, which is a DAG.

concepts.name: Kosaraju's algorithm
concepts.statement: DFS the graph and order vertices by decreasing exit time; then DFS the transposed graph in that order, and each tree is an SCC. Correct because for an edge C -> C' of the condensation, tout[C] > tout[C']; O(n + m).

concepts.name: Tarjan's SCC algorithm
concepts.statement: One DFS with a stack and low values; a vertex with low[v] = tin[v] is the root of an SCC, which is popped off the stack; O(n + m).

concepts.name: Building the condensation graph
concepts.statement: Map each vertex to its component's root and add an edge between roots for every edge crossing components.

concepts.name: Strong orientation
concepts.statement: An undirected connected graph can be oriented to be strongly connected iff it has no bridges (Robbins); orienting tree edges down and back edges up in a DFS does it, and minimising SCCs in general takes components + bridges.

concepts.name: Single-source shortest paths problem
concepts.statement: Given a weighted graph and source s, find the length (and a path) of the shortest path from s to every vertex.

concepts.name: Dijkstra's algorithm
concepts.statement: With non-negative weights, repeatedly mark the unmarked vertex of least tentative distance and relax its out-edges; once marked, a vertex's distance is final (proof by induction), so all distances are found; O(n^2 + m) with a linear scan, optimal for dense graphs.
concepts.notes: article ends with 38 practice-problem links; proof at #proof

concepts.name: Edge relaxation and predecessor array
concepts.statement: Relaxing (v, to, w) sets d[to] = d[v] + w and p[to] = v when this improves d[to]; following p from the target restores a shortest path.

concepts.name: Dijkstra with a priority queue or set
concepts.statement: On sparse graphs keep (distance, vertex) pairs in a set (erasing the old pair on improvement) or a priority queue with lazy deletion (skip entries whose distance is stale), giving O(m log n).
concepts.notes: no practice links; set at #set, priority_queue at #priority_queue

concepts.name: Bellman-Ford algorithm
concepts.statement: Relax every edge in n-1 phases; after phase i all shortest paths of at most i edges are correct, so with no reachable negative cycle all distances are exact in O(nm); stopping early when a phase changes nothing.
concepts.notes: article ends with 8 practice-problem links (heading 'Related problems in online judges'); proof at #the-proof-of-the-algorithm

concepts.name: Negative cycle detection with Bellman-Ford
concepts.statement: If some edge still relaxes in an n-th phase, a negative cycle is reachable; walking n predecessor steps back from that vertex lands on the cycle, which is then read off.

concepts.name: Shortest Path Faster Algorithm (SPFA)
concepts.statement: Queue only vertices whose distance just improved; worst case still O(nm), often much faster; counting relaxations per vertex (n) detects negative cycles.

concepts.name: 0-1 BFS
concepts.statement: With edge weights 0 or 1, a deque replaces the priority queue: push to the front after a 0-edge relaxation and to the back after a 1-edge; this is Dijkstra in O(n + m).

concepts.name: Dial's algorithm
concepts.statement: With integer weights at most k, k+1 buckets of vertices indexed by distance modulo k+1 replace the priority queue.

concepts.name: D'Esopo-Pape algorithm
concepts.statement: Keep vertices in three sets (done, in deque, untouched); a vertex re-improved after being processed goes to the front of the deque, a new one to the back; usually faster than Dijkstra and Bellman-Ford but exponential in the worst case.

concepts.name: Floyd-Warshall algorithm
concepts.statement: Before phase k, d[i][j] is the shortest i->j path using only intermediate vertices < k; d[i][j] = min(d[i][j], d[i][k] + d[k][j]) over k, i, j yields all-pairs distances in O(n^3) when no negative cycles exist.

concepts.name: Restoring Floyd-Warshall paths
concepts.statement: Store the phase k that last improved d[i][j] and recurse on (i, k) and (k, j).

concepts.name: Floyd-Warshall with negative cycles
concepts.statement: After running, d[t][t] < 0 marks t on a negative cycle; any pair (i, j) with d[i][t] < INF and d[t][j] < INF for such t has no shortest path (minus infinity).

concepts.name: Counting paths of fixed length by matrix power
concepts.statement: The (i, j) entry of the k-th power of the adjacency matrix counts walks of exactly k edges from i to j; binary exponentiation gives O(n^3 log k).

concepts.name: Shortest paths of fixed length by min-plus product
concepts.statement: Replacing (+, *) by (min, +) in matrix multiplication, the k-th power of the weight matrix gives shortest walks of exactly k edges in O(n^3 log k); adding a copy vertex with a 0-loop extends to at most k edges.

concepts.name: Minimum spanning tree
concepts.statement: A spanning tree (n-1 edges connecting all vertices with no cycle) of a weighted undirected graph with least total weight.

concepts.name: Prim's algorithm
concepts.statement: Grow one tree from an arbitrary vertex, always adding the cheapest edge leaving it (an exchange argument shows the result is minimal); O(n^2) with per-vertex minimum edges for dense graphs, O(m log n) with a set/heap for sparse ones.
concepts.notes: no practice links; proof at #proof; dense at #dense-graphs-on2, sparse at #sparse-graphs-om-log-n

concepts.name: Properties of minimum spanning trees
concepts.statement: An MST is unique if all weights are distinct; with positive weights it also minimises the product of weights; and it minimises the maximum edge weight among spanning trees (minimum bottleneck).

concepts.name: Kruskal's algorithm
concepts.statement: Sort edges by weight and add each edge whose endpoints lie in different trees; correctness by an exchange argument; O(m log n + n^2) with a naive tree-id array.
concepts.notes: article ends with 28 practice-problem links; proof at #proof-of-correctness

concepts.name: Kruskal with DSU
concepts.statement: Use DSU find to test and union to merge trees, giving O(m log n) dominated by sorting; stop after n-1 edges.
concepts.notes: 0 links of its own (points to Kruskal article's list); near-duplicate of mst_kruskal#improved-implementation

concepts.name: Second-best MST is one edge swap from the MST
concepts.statement: Some second-best spanning tree differs from a given MST by exactly one edge replacement, so it suffices to try removing one tree edge or adding one non-tree edge.

concepts.name: Second-best minimum spanning tree
concepts.statement: The second-best MST differs from the MST by one edge swap; adding each non-tree edge (u, v) and removing the heaviest tree edge on the u-v path (found with binary lifting / LCA) gives it in O(m log n).

concepts.name: Kirchhoff's matrix tree theorem
concepts.statement: The number of spanning trees of a multigraph equals any cofactor of its Laplacian L = D - A, e.g. the determinant after deleting one row and column; computed by Gaussian elimination in O(n^3).
concepts.notes: article ends with 3 practice-problem links; no code; relation to circuit laws at #relation-to-kirchhoffs-circuit-laws

concepts.name: Prufer code
concepts.statement: Encode a labelled tree on n vertices as n-2 numbers by repeatedly removing the smallest-numbered leaf and writing down its neighbour; each vertex appears degree-1 times.

concepts.name: Prufer code and tree restoration in linear time
concepts.statement: A moving pointer to the smallest leaf works because only the just-reduced neighbour can become a new smaller leaf; the same trick rebuilds the tree from the code via the degrees, both O(n) (O(n log n) with a heap).

concepts.name: Cayley's formula
concepts.statement: Prufer codes biject labelled trees with sequences of n-2 values in [0, n-1], so the complete graph K_n has n^(n-2) spanning trees.

concepts.name: Ways to make a graph connected
concepts.statement: A graph with k components of sizes s1..sk can be made connected by adding k-1 edges in s1 s2 ... sk n^(k-2) ways (via Prufer codes and the multinomial theorem).

concepts.name: Cycle detection and finding with DFS colours
concepts.statement: With white/grey/black colouring, a directed graph has a cycle iff DFS meets an edge into a grey vertex (in an undirected graph, any visited vertex other than the parent); the cycle is read from the parent array, in O(M).
concepts.notes: article ends with 3 practice-problem links; short

concepts.name: Finding any negative cycle
concepts.statement: Initialise all d to 0 (a virtual source to every vertex) and run Bellman-Ford n phases; a vertex relaxed in the last phase leads back to a negative cycle; Floyd-Warshall's negative diagonal finds all pairs without a shortest path.
concepts.notes: article ends with 3 practice-problem links; largely duplicates bellman_ford#the-case-of-a-negative-cycle and floyd-warshall#the-case-of-negative-cycles

concepts.name: Existence of Eulerian path/cycle
concepts.statement: A connected (ignoring isolated vertices) undirected multigraph has an Eulerian cycle iff all degrees are even, and an Eulerian path iff exactly zero or two vertices have odd degree.

concepts.name: Finding an Eulerian path in O(M)
concepts.statement: Walk unused edges from a vertex, pushing vertices on a stack and emitting each when it has no unused edges; this splices simple cycles into one Euler cycle; for a path, add an edge between the two odd vertices first and cut there.
concepts.notes: domino problem at #the-domino-problem; code uses an adjacency matrix

concepts.name: Lowest common ancestor
concepts.statement: For vertices u, v of a rooted tree, the deepest vertex that is an ancestor of both (a vertex counts as its own ancestor).

concepts.name: LCA via Euler tour and range minimum
concepts.statement: Record the DFS Euler tour (2n-1 entries) with depths and each vertex's first occurrence; LCA(u, v) is the minimum-depth vertex between first[u] and first[v], so LCA reduces to RMQ (segment tree: O(log N) per query; sqrt decomposition: O(sqrt N)).

concepts.name: Binary lifting for LCA
concepts.statement: Precompute up[v][j], the 2^j-th ancestor, by DFS in O(N log N); with entry/exit times, lift u by decreasing powers while the ancestor is not an ancestor of v, answering LCA in O(log N).

concepts.name: Binary lifting with depths (supports adding leaves)
concepts.statement: Equalise depths by lifting the deeper vertex depth[u]-depth[v] steps, then lift both while their ancestors differ; new leaves only need their own up[] row.

concepts.name: LCA with O(n) space jump pointers
concepts.statement: Each vertex keeps its parent and one 'big' jump defined recursively from its parent's jumps (skew-binary); level ancestor and LCA queries run in O(log n) with O(n) space and preprocessing.

concepts.name: Farach-Colton and Bender LCA
concepts.statement: On the Euler tour depths (adjacent values differ by 1), split into blocks of size 0.5 log N; a sparse table over block minima plus precomputed answers for each of the O(sqrt N) possible +-1 block shapes give O(N) preprocessing and O(1) queries.

concepts.name: Static RMQ in O(N)/O(1) via Cartesian tree
concepts.statement: Build the min-Cartesian tree of the array with a stack in O(N); RMQ(L, R) is the LCA of L and R, answered in O(1) by Farach-Colton and Bender.

concepts.name: Tarjan's offline LCA
concepts.statement: One DFS with DSU: after finishing a child, union it into the current vertex and set the set's ancestor to the current vertex; a query (u, v) answered at u when v is visited is ancestor[find(v)]; O(n + m) total with DSU in alpha.
concepts.notes: no practice links; DSU article also links this at disjoint_set_union#offline-lca-lowest-common-ancestor-in-a-tree-in-oalphan-on-average

concepts.name: Flow network, flow and residual network
concepts.statement: A directed graph with capacities and a source and sink; a flow respects capacities and conserves flow at inner vertices; the residual network holds capacity minus flow on each edge plus the flow as capacity on its reverse.

concepts.name: Ford-Fulkerson method
concepts.statement: While the residual network has an s-t path, push its bottleneck capacity along it (updating reverse edges); with integer capacities it terminates in O(E F).

concepts.name: Edmonds-Karp algorithm
concepts.statement: Ford-Fulkerson with BFS (shortest augmenting paths) runs in O(V E^2) independent of the flow value, since each augmentation saturates an edge and s-t distances never decrease.

concepts.name: Integral flow theorem
concepts.statement: If all capacities are integers there is a maximum flow with integer flow on every edge (and Ford-Fulkerson finds one).

concepts.name: Max-flow min-cut theorem
concepts.statement: The maximum s-t flow equals the minimum capacity of an s-t cut; after max flow, the vertices reachable from s in the residual network form a minimum cut.

concepts.name: Preflow, excess and valid labeling
concepts.statement: A preflow obeys capacities but lets inflow exceed outflow (excess x(u) > 0 marks an active vertex); a valid labeling h has h(s) = |V|, h(t) = 0 and h(u) <= h(v) + 1 for every residual edge (u, v).

concepts.name: Push-relabel maximum flow
concepts.statement: Start with a preflow saturating source edges and heights h(s)=|V|; push excess along admissible residual edges (h(u) = h(v)+1) and relabel when none exists; O(V^2) relabels and O(VE) saturating pushes give O(V^2 E) with a FIFO of active vertices.
concepts.notes: uses a current-arc structure; complexity at #complexity

concepts.name: Highest-label push-relabel
concepts.statement: Always discharging an active vertex of greatest height reduces the bound to O(VE + V^2 sqrt E), i.e. O(V^3) worst case.
concepts.notes: no practice links; very short article, a delta on push-relabel

concepts.name: Dinic's algorithm
concepts.statement: In phases, build the BFS level graph of the residual network and find a blocking flow by DFS with per-vertex edge pointers; fewer than V phases as dist(s,t) strictly grows, giving O(V^2 E).
concepts.notes: article ends with 1 practice-problem link; proofs at #proof-of-correctness, #number-of-phases

concepts.name: Dinic on unit networks
concepts.statement: On unit networks (each inner vertex has a single in- or out-edge, unit capacities) Dinic runs in O(E sqrt V); on general unit-capacity networks phases are O(sqrt E) and O(V^(2/3)).

concepts.name: MPM maximum flow
concepts.statement: Like Dinic but finds each blocking flow by repeatedly saturating the vertex of minimum potential min(in-capacity, out-capacity) in the layered network, giving O(V^3).

concepts.name: Flows with lower bounds (demands)
concepts.statement: Edges with demand d(e) <= f(e) <= c(e): add s', t', edges s'->v and v->t' carrying the demands, capacities c - d and an infinite t->s edge; a feasible flow exists iff the max s'-t' flow saturates all new edges; binary search on the t->s capacity gives the minimal flow.

concepts.name: Minimal flow with demands by binary search
concepts.statement: The infinite t->s edge carries the original network's flow; binary searching its capacity for the smallest value that still saturates the new edges gives the minimum feasible flow.

concepts.name: Minimum-cost flow by successive shortest paths
concepts.statement: Repeatedly augment along a cheapest s-t path in the residual network (reverse edges cost -c) until the required flow K is sent; O(F nm) with Bellman-Ford/SPFA, faster with Dijkstra and Johnson potentials.
concepts.notes: article ends with 3 practice-problem links; undirected/multigraph handling at #undirected-graphs-multigraphs

concepts.name: Assignment problem via min-cost flow
concepts.statement: Build source -> N workers -> N jobs -> sink with unit capacities and assignment costs on middle edges; a min-cost maximum flow of value N is an optimal assignment.

concepts.name: Global minimum cut
concepts.statement: In an undirected weighted graph, a non-empty proper vertex subset minimising the total weight of edges leaving it, with no fixed source or sink; solvable by O(n^2) max flows but faster directly.

concepts.name: Stoer-Wagner global minimum cut
concepts.statement: In each of n-1 phases grow a set A by the most tightly connected vertex; the last two added vertices s, t have min s-t cut equal to the weight of t's edges into A (Stoer-Wagner theorem); record it and merge s and t; O(n^3) simply, O(nm + n^2 log n) with a heap.

concepts.name: Bipartiteness check by BFS 2-colouring
concepts.statement: A graph is bipartite iff it has no odd cycle; BFS from each unvisited vertex colours vertices alternately and fails exactly when an edge joins two vertices of the same colour, in O(n + m).
concepts.notes: article ends with 6 practice-problem links; short

concepts.name: Matching, maximal and maximum matching, augmenting path
concepts.statement: A matching is a set of pairwise non-adjacent edges; maximal means no edge can be added, maximum means largest cardinality; an augmenting path alternates non-matching/matching edges between two unsaturated vertices.

concepts.name: Berge's lemma
concepts.statement: A matching is maximum iff no augmenting path exists relative to it; flipping an augmenting path increases the matching by one.

concepts.name: Kuhn's algorithm for maximum bipartite matching
concepts.statement: For each left vertex, search by DFS (try_kuhn) for an augmenting path and flip it; O(n1 m), so put the smaller part on the left; a greedy initial matching speeds it up.
concepts.notes: improved version at #improved-implementation; notes mention Hopcroft-Karp and Konig's theorem

concepts.name: Assignment problem
concepts.statement: Given an n x n cost matrix, choose one entry in each row and column (a permutation) minimising the total; equivalently a minimum-weight perfect matching in a complete bipartite graph.

concepts.name: Hungarian algorithm
concepts.statement: Maintain potentials u, v with u[i] + v[j] <= A[i][j] (a lower bound by duality) and grow the matching along tight edges, adjusting potentials when stuck; adding rows one at a time with per-column minima gives O(n^2 m) (O(n^3)).
concepts.notes: O(n^4) at #the-mathcalon4-algorithm, O(n^3) at #the-mathcalon3-algorithm; link to SSP at #connection-to-the-successive-shortest-path-algorithm

concepts.name: Topological order
concepts.statement: An ordering of the vertices of a directed graph in which every edge goes from an earlier to a later vertex; it exists iff the graph is acyclic and need not be unique.

concepts.name: Topological sort by DFS
concepts.statement: In a DAG, appending each vertex when its DFS call finishes and reversing the list yields an order in which every edge goes forward; O(n + m).

concepts.name: Edge and vertex connectivity
concepts.statement: Edge connectivity lambda (vertex connectivity kappa) is the fewest edges (vertices) whose removal disconnects the graph; it equals the minimum over pairs s, t of an s-t separating set's size.

concepts.name: Whitney inequalities
concepts.statement: kappa <= lambda <= delta, where delta is the minimum degree, and these cannot be improved in general.

concepts.name: Computing connectivity with max flow
concepts.statement: By Menger/Ford-Fulkerson, the max number of edge-disjoint s-t paths is a unit-capacity max flow; minimise over pairs (or use Stoer-Wagner); for vertex connectivity split each vertex into in/out with capacity 1.

concepts.name: Counting painted edges on tree paths with Euler tour
concepts.statement: Split a path at the LCA into two ancestor-descendant paths; over the Euler tour keep segment trees of forward and backward edge colours, so the count on an ancestor path is T1[p..q-1] - T2[p..q-1], O(log N) per query and paint.

concepts.name: 2-CNF and the implication graph
concepts.statement: In 2-SAT every clause has two literals; each clause (a or b) is equivalent to not a -> b and not b -> a, giving a directed graph on 2n literal vertices.

concepts.name: 2-SAT
concepts.statement: Turn each clause (a or b) into implications not a -> b and not b -> a; the formula is satisfiable iff no variable shares an SCC with its negation, and setting x true iff comp[x] comes after comp[not x] in topological order gives an assignment; O(n + m).

concepts.name: Heavy-light decomposition
concepts.statement: Mark the edge to a child with subtree at least half (or the largest) as heavy; heavy edges form disjoint paths and any root path crosses O(log n) light edges, so path queries split into O(log n) path segments.
concepts.notes: article ends with 7 practice-problem links; proof at #proof-of-correctness

concepts.name: Path queries with HLD and segment trees
concepts.statement: Lay heavy paths contiguously in one segment tree; max/sum queries and repainting on the path a-b take O(log^2 n) by walking both ends up chain by chain.

concepts.name: Centroid of a tree
concepts.statement: A vertex whose removal leaves no component with more than n/2 vertices; every tree has one or two, and two centroids are adjacent.
concepts.notes: article ends with 6 practice-problem links; existence proof at #existence-and-uniqueness

concepts.name: Centroid decomposition
concepts.statement: Recursively remove a centroid and decompose the remaining components; the recursion depth is O(log N) and every path passes through the centroid of some component, so path-counting problems run in O(N log N) times per-level work.
concepts.notes: finding a centroid at #finding-a-centroid; example counts paths of length K
